reverse_outline.summary: Three takeaways: approval is a promise not money, no step is final, each promise has an owner, clock and price
Opening case: an approved, paid-out class pass is clawed back by a chargeback weeks later though nothing failed
A card payment is a chain of separate promises by different parties on different clocks, none of which makes it final
One status word cannot represent facts held by four different parties, so a single-status system is wrong for days
Roadmap of the part: the five chapters in payment order and the three integrator beliefs they overturn
Chapter 1 preview: the whole journey as six steps among five parties, with the provider controlling none of the deciding steps
Chapter 2 preview: authorization is the issuer's time-limited promise that moves no money, and a timeout is an unknown outcome
Chapter 3 preview: how capture, clearing, netting and payout move money over days, so 'settled' means different events to different parties
Chapter 4 preview: three routes for money going back (reversal, refund, dispute), each with a different owner and a long dispute window
Chapter 5 preview: the fee splits into interchange, scheme fees and provider markup, and pricing models decide which costs are visible
What the reader can do after the part and how to read it: in order, or jump to the chapter matching a question

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All ten outline summaries match the controlling ideas of the spec paragraphs they are aligned to (p01 to p10), in the spec's order; the callout matches no paragraph and carries the thesis statement as the spec places it.
The outliner needed one phrase for every unit; no unit was marked as holding two ideas.
p01 to p04 perform the hook, claim, reason and roadmap of the part thesis; p05 to p09 each introduce the chapter that argues one of P1-1 to P1-5; p10 is the synthesis.

Each scenario, fact, figure and the one quotation is tied to a stated point: 'No step of the payment had failed.' (p01), 'that right outlasts them all' (p02), both figure captions, 'No status word answers that.' after the owner's question (p05), 'All three are right' (p07), 'stays open until at least 2 June 2027' (p08). Borderline, passed: the Stripe and Adyen sentence in p07 leans on the two sentences before it ('on its own schedule', 'a different event ... at the provider') and one flow reader (A, item 11) could not tell which point it illustrates.

Every declared boundary is expressed and picks up the declared known information: 'Nothing had failed, yet the money came back.' (p02, elaboration); 'No status can hold these promises, because ...' (p03, cause-effect); 'Part I follows the payment in the order it happens.' (p04, sequence); 'opens the first step' (p06); 'turns to the steps that do move money' (p07, contrast); 'begins after the payout' (p08, time); 'comes last: a fee can be assigned to a party and a step only once you know both' (p09, cause-effect); 'Read in that order, the five chapters turn ...' (conclusion). The section's transition sentence 'Below, each gets a paragraph ...' states the elaboration, but its 'each' is misread; that is ruled under intro_predicts_content and flow_is_followable.

results.quote: No status can hold these promises, because each belongs to a party other than the provider, with its own record and clock
results.finding: Contradicts the paragraph before, which lists the payout among the four promises as the provider's own ('the provider pays the merchant on its own schedule'); both readers stopped on 'each'. The spec's p03 controlling idea makes the same overstatement ('each of those promises belongs to a party other than the provider') while p02 counts the provider's payout as a promise, so the fix is a changed claim.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 4 (reported by flow reader A, item 4)

results.quote: Three integrator beliefs are overturned: that approved means paid, that paid out means final, that the fee is one charge. Below, each gets a paragraph: its question in bold, its argument and its Larkfield case.
results.finding: 'each' attaches to the three beliefs in the sentence just before it, so both readers expected three paragraphs, met five and went back. Naming the referent ('each chapter') or moving the beliefs sentence ahead of the chapter list fixes it within the word limit.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 5 (reported by flow reader A, item 7; the intro reader made the same misreading)

results.quote: Its answer is six steps over days (the four promises, a clearing record, the dispute window) by at least five parties: first a message moves, then a record, then money.
results.finding: Four counts arrive in two sentences (six steps, at least five parties, a three-part sequence, then 'the three steps that decide the outcome') after the introduction and Figure 1 fixed four promises by four parties; both readers re-read and could not map five parties onto four or the three-part sequence onto the six steps. The spec requires all of these in p05 and 'four facts held by four parties' in p03, and the page has one word left, so reconciling them needs words or content the spec does not allow.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, items 6 and 7 (reported by flow reader A, item 8)

results.quote: Ask any provider first: which legal entity is the acquirer in this country?
results.finding: A paragraph that describes a chapter and its case ends on an instruction to the reader with no reason given; both readers called it out of place. Presenting it as what the chapter gives (its first question to put to a provider) keeps the spec's evidence and removes the jolt.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 8 (reported by flow reader A, item 9)

results.quote: (the four promises, a clearing record, the dispute window)
results.finding: 'clearing' is on the spec's does_not_know list and is to be glossed in a clause; it is used in the roadmap (p04) and here with no gloss, and what the record is becomes clear only in p07 ('the acquirer presents a clearing record through the network').
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A, item 8 and flow reader B, item 6 (both: 'a clearing record' is not explained here)

results.quote: the banks settle through the card network a day or more later
results.finding: 'card network' is on the spec's does_not_know list and the page never glosses it or says that Visa is one. Fault is unclear: either the draft owes a clause, or the list is over-inclusive (the preface chapters use the term repeatedly and the reader called it easy to guess).
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 2; the term is on does_not_know and the draft never gives it

results.finding: The body opens on a dated scene with amounts, not on a placeholder, a restated question, a definition, a 'dawn of man' sweep or a book report.

The conclusion does not open with 'in conclusion', adds no new subtopic, holds no body evidence and does not end on a rephrased thesis: it ends on a course of action and the hand-off 'Begin with [[journey-of-a-payment]].'

Synthesis no single chapter paragraph states: 'the five chapters turn Bram's €120 from a surprise into a sequence'; so-what: 'By the end you can name each party that said yes on 2 February, what each was paid for saying it, and why none of those yeses stopped the chargeback', and 'With one question in hand, about a status, a delay, a reversal or a fee, open the chapter that answers it.'
Returns to Bram de Wit's €120 of p01 with both of its dates: 'said yes on 2 February ... the chargeback of 24 February'.

results.quote: I expect the rest of this page to take three questions in turn, one paragraph each, each overturning one integrator belief: that approved means paid, that paid out means final, and that the fee is one charge.
results.finding: The quote is the intro reader's prediction. The roadmap promises one paragraph per chapter, five in payment order; the reader predicted three paragraphs on the three beliefs and said the introduction 'gives two orders' and that 'each gets a paragraph' could refer to either. Claim, the five chapters' order for the part, kind of evidence and tone were predicted correctly. Same cause and same fix as the flow finding on 'Below, each gets a paragraph'.

The probe answer states the claim (a chain of separate promises by different parties on different clocks, none of which makes the payment final) and the five chapters in order with their subjects: the whole path and its parties, what an authorization promises, how clearing and settlement move the money, how refunds, reversals and disputes move it back, where the fee goes. It matches `expected`.

The first body paragraph is the scene itself: 'On 2 February 2027 a ten-class pass for €120.00 is bought with Bram de Wit's card at Studio Noord', 'On 24 February a chargeback arrives', 'a €15.00 dispute fee (illustrative)', with Larkfield named 'the fictional studio-software platform this book follows'. The KEY POINTS callout above it is where the spec places the thesis statement; it is not a description of the part.
